title.en: Universal franchise and India's electoral system

text.en: In 1949 a member of the Constituent Assembly said that India adopted adult franchise with great faith in the common man, an experiment never so boldly tried before.

Franchise is the right to vote, and universal adult franchise means every adult citizen gets one vote and all votes are equal in value.
Every Indian citizen aged 18 or above can vote, regardless of caste, religion, gender, education or wealth.
No one can vote on another person's behalf, and the vote is secret.
Before Independence only about 13 per cent of Indians could vote, but India gave women the vote from the very beginning of the Republic.
Article 326 of the Constitution provides universal franchise for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
India holds elections at three levels: the Lok Sabha, state legislative assemblies and local bodies like panchayats and municipalities.
The country is divided into constituencies, and in each constituency the candidate with the most votes wins, called first past the post.
The Election Commission of India is an independent body that conducts free and fair elections.
Voters are listed in an electoral roll, vote using Electronic Voting Machines, and political parties must follow a Model Code of Conduct.
Voting is both a right and a duty, and informed voters make democracy strong.

problem.en: Who can vote in India, and who cannot?

text.en: Every citizen aged 18 or more is eligible, with the name on the electoral roll.
People below 18 and non-citizens cannot vote.
Caste, religion, gender and wealth do not matter.

prompt.en: Why is the vote called equal?

requiredIdeas.en: Every vote has the same value.

points.en: Universal adult franchise gives every citizen aged 18 or more one equal vote.
The Election Commission conducts free and fair elections.
Elections happen at national, state and local levels.
